title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
abstract: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once. In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang. Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry ; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league. In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.” Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night. “Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday . When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.” “Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”

title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
abstract: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks. Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year. Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed. In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

title: Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
abstract: A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon. The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public. “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says. Huang resigned on Thursday , four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs . Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding .

title: An overview of Jensen Huang’s messy days
abstract: The Stepback Column AI Tech An overview of Jensen Huang’s messy days Things moved fast for the now-former CEO of Nvidia. by Terrence O'Brien Nov 15, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. This is The Stepback , a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien . The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here . How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, previously told The Verge . “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “ close relationship ” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024 . Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions . Meanwhile, he had gotten quite cozy with President Trump, once even putting him on speakerphone on-stage at the All-In Summit. Then last week, things escalated quickly. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review , 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015 , which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider .) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg , he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “ extraordinarily difficult period .” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th . It closed at $162.85 on November 13th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China , and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “ completely normal and not unusual .” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “ national security concerns ” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters , Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense . Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “ sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity ,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “ be an honor ” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “ bring back THE boss ,” on an internal post. Some even speculated that Jensen Huang was the victim of a vast conspiracy , whether that was a coup by some faction within Nvidia, or perhaps the goal of China all along had simply been to chase him from the CEO chair . By Thursday night, Reuters reported a third affair , this one also with an Nvidia employee, though no further information has emerged. What happens next First and foremost for Nvidia, it must find a new CEO. It’s possible that Kress eventually ceases to be “interim” CEO, but other names, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji , have also been rumored. (Donald Trump believes they should hire Tim Cook , but to call that unlikely would be an understatement.) It’s also possible that Nvidia will undergo a dramatic reorganization. Whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to keep the 60 direct reports of Jensen Huang. With a first-ever board chair in Jones, it’s also possible that the board of directors will play a larger role in the company going forward. The board’s investigation into Jensen Huang that began on November 8th is ongoing. The scandal is likely to drag on for some time .

title: Bland Launches Tofu-1, a Full-Duplex Speech-to-Speech Model for Calls
abstract: Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, has released Tofu-1 , a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview. The Tofu-1 speech-to-speech model targets calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines. It listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out, with no transcript between. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models. Most voice agents are cascades. They turn speech into text, pass it to a language model, then turn the reply back into speech. Tofu-1 listens to the audio directly , so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland has not published the internal architecture. Bland lists 3 audio skills on its product page: Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early. Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise. The TV Test asks one question: can the model follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene? TV audio is often louder than the caller. Bland marks its TV Test walkthrough as illustrative, not recorded model output. Competitor figures come from each vendor’s own page. FDB results use different benchmark versions and are not directly comparable. Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises. Bland names banking, healthcare, insurance and government as target sectors. The sign-up form asks for monthly call volume, from under 1,000 to 50,000+. title: 🗞️Nvidia Without Jensen, Alibaba’s Chip IPO, and Qwen4’s First Look
abstract: China AI Weekly Digest summarizes the week’s big news, model updates, compute, policy, products, and research, drawn from the China AI Index newsfeed . The digest is (mostly) compiled and drafted by an AI agent using credible news outlets; I fact-check and edit it. Read to the end for “One to Watch” as this week’s video pick. This week: 248 stories tracked (0 editor picks, 99 English-language, 149 Chinese-language 🇨🇳) over 2026-11-07–2026-11-14. Alibaba discloses a Hong Kong listing application for its chip unit. Alibaba said on November 10 that T-Head had confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing on September 11. T-Head designs chips for data-center workloads, making it part of Alibaba’s own effort to build out AI infrastructure. A listing would give investors a separate way to value that chip business while keeping it within the group, as Alibaba expects T-Head to remain a subsidiary. Final offering terms, including how much the unit might raise, are still pending. ( SCMP / 雷峰網 / HKEX ) MiniMax and ByteDance give image generation a production workflow. MiniMax released H3 Image with open weights and made it available through its API, MiniMax Code and Hailuo. The model generates images at native 4K and accepts up to 16 references, giving users more control over which elements carry into the result. ByteDance began rolling Seedream 5.5 into Doubao, Doubao Work and Jimeng, with localized edits and support for generating images with transparent backgrounds. ( 量子位 / 雷峰網 / @MiniMax_AI / @BytePlusGlobal ) Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia faces renewed scrutiny over chip exports and mounting U.S.–China tensions. Nvidia said Huang stepped down as CEO and from its board effective November 11, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. The board has launched an independent investigation into allegations surrounding Huang and Nvidia’s China business. Huang’s departure could reshape the global AI landscape, particularly U.S.–China technology competition. A vocal opponent of restricting chip sales to China, Huang had argued that keeping Chinese developers within Nvidia’s ecosystem served American interests. His exit comes as bipartisan lawmakers push for tighter export controls, including potential restrictions on overseas cloud access to advanced AI chips. ( Nvidia 8-K / Reuters ) This week brought downloadable weights from Meituan, a new speech model from Tencent and previews from Baidu and Qwen. Meituan published the LongCat-2.5 weights under the MIT license, giving developers a way to run or adapt the multimodal model themselves. Meituan lists 1.6 trillion total parameters and about 48 billion active per token, with the model built for tasks that combine visual understanding and agentic coding. ( VentureBeat ) Baidu introduced ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview, a separate release from ERNIE 5.5 Base. Its demonstrations focused on practical tasks, including generating interactive 3D scenes through code and handling knowledge-work assignments. ( 雷峰網 ) Tencent released Hy Realtime, a Hunyuan speech model for live voice interaction. The model takes speech input and generates spoken responses, giving developers a model designed for conversational audio. ( 第一財經 / IT之家 ) Alibaba previewed Qwen4-Max, the first model in its next-generation Qwen4 family, on November 11. The multimodal model supports text, image and video inputs, a 1 million-token context window, and reasoning capabilities designed for coding, complex agentic tasks and knowledge work. ( @Alibaba_Qwen ) BytePlus announced Seedance 2.5 Flash and quoted US$0.152 per second for 720p text-to-video and image-to-video. It says Flash is nearly twice as fast as the flagship. ( @BytePlusGlobal ) Server makers moved toward public markets while policymakers looked at who can buy advanced chips and where those chips end up. Chinese AI server maker xFusion cleared a Shenzhen Stock Exchange review for its proposed ChiNext listing, Reuters reported. The planned offering is sized at about US$1.2 billion, and the review clears one stage of the listing process. ( Reuters ) SMIC expects tight AI computing supply to persist until 2028, according to SCMP. The foundry’s forecast puts a timeframe on the capacity pressure facing AI developers as Washington weighs tighter controls on advanced chips. ( SCMP ) Malaysia is considering closer oversight of data centers to curb the resale and diversion of advanced AI chips, Caixin reported. The proposal would bring data-center operators into the enforcement picture by focusing on what happens to chips after they enter the country. ( 財新 ) U.S. Senator Tom Cotton urged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to block Chinese DRAM maker CXMT from the U.S. market. The request targets access to U.S. buyers and would require action by the administration. ( Reuters / CNBC ) Kimi’s maker took preparatory steps toward a listing, while two robotics rounds funded manufacturing and factory deployments. Moonshot AI is restructuring ahead of a potential IPO, the WSJ reported. The Kimi developer is moving shareholder interests from a Cayman Islands structure into a Chinese entity. The Journal put its latest private valuation at US$50 billion. ( WSJ ) UniX AI closed a RMB500 million pre-A round, with Greenland Group joining as a strategic investor. The Suzhou robotics company says the money will help it scale production and deliveries of its general-purpose humanoids. ( 投資界 / 新京報貝殼財經 ) Zhifeng Chuangyuan raised RMB80 million in an angel round. The company has introduced its wheeled, dual-arm Z100 and plans to spend the money on R&D and expansion into optical-module manufacturing, where robots need to perform precise insertion and removal tasks. ( 投資界 ) Beijing set a robot manufacturing target, Shanghai laid out rules for scientific data, and U.S.–China safety talks surfaced a basic question about incident reporting. Beijing’s 2026–2028 embodied robotics plan calls for local production capacity of 200,000 finished robots a year. The city will support both contract manufacturing and companies’ own production lines, alongside shared facilities across Beijing, Tianjin and Hebei to speed up parts prototyping. ( 財聯社 / 北京市政府 ) Shanghai issued trial rules on preserving, classifying and sharing scientific data. The measures also encourage research institutions and AI developers to work together, putting scientific datasets within reach of more model-development projects where sharing is permitted. ( 第一財經 / 上海市科委 ) Washington and Beijing established a channel to discuss risks from advanced AI. Analysts told SCMP that agreeing on what counts as a “serious” incident could be an early hurdle. That definition would shape which events either government is expected to bring to the other’s attention. ( SCMP ) DeepSeek opened up tools from its consumer app, while Qwen added an agent that colleagues can use together. DeepSeek opened APIs for capabilities already used in its app, including search, document and link ingestion, voice and safety checks. Developers can also call standalone services for optical character recognition, speech recognition and speech synthesis. ( 第一財經 / @deepseek_ai ) Qwen Office 2.0 introduced Team Agent, a shared workspace where colleagues can work with the same assistant. A group can bring its own materials into a shared task and collaborate on the output in that workspace. ( 量子位 / 雷峰網 ) Apple completed Chinese generative-AI service filings covering tablets and laptops. The filings extend the registered device categories for Apple Intelligence. The report gave no rollout date for either category. ( 第一財經 ) Robot teams tested how touch and movement transfer across hardware and environments, while a new drug-discovery model took on biomolecular benchmarks. Ant-backed Robbyant’s LingBot-Touch learns a common representation across pressure-sensitive, magnetic and camera-based tactile sensors.

title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
abstract: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings. Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms. But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis. Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover different positional methods in LLMs; what methods are used by recent open LLMs. Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) . If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher: The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style. PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses. PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures . Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here , which also has a navigation bar on the left side. Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token. The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation. A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention. We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed. Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example: “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.” Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure. For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7. (If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub .) Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer. Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair. GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.) Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information. If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article. We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information. The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections. To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block. The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation: And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and x m the token ID at that position. The input to the first block is E token is the embedding layer, P m is the position info vector selected by m , and h m is the resulting summed embedding and position vector. The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise.

AI Agent》 後，在與讀者交流的過程中，我越來越感到：要開發好基於模型的應用，還需要理解它賴以執行的基礎設施。大多數軟體工程師不必親自開發作業系統、編譯器和晶片，卻仍要學習作業系統、編譯原理和計算機體系結構，因為申請記憶體、讀取檔案、呼叫函式，背後都有資源與時間代價。基於模型開發應用也是如此。延遲相差幾倍，產品體驗就可能完全不同；成本相差一個數量級，能夠支撐的商業模式也隨之改變。 更深層的變化是 程式設計抽象的上移：從作業系統到模型上下文 。傳統的作業系統、編譯器和硬體要為事先未知的各種程式提供通用能力，系統最佳化總要在可程式設計性與效能之間取捨。如今 LLM 成了最重要的應用，從運算元執行到分散式排程，都可以針對特定的模型和加速器架構最佳化；模型設計也開始反過來適應硬體，DeepSeek V4/V4.1 重新設計長上下文的表示方式，就是一例。從某種意義上說， 模型成了 LLM 時代的作業系統，AI Infra 成了 LLM 時代的計算機體系結構 。《計算機體系結構：量化研究方法》是我在體系結構領域的入門書，而 AI Infra 領域還缺少一本從硬體約束和模型架構出發、量化推導系統設計的書，這是我寫作本書的動機。 貫穿全書的方法是 從約束推導設計 ：先明確任務與質量要求，列出計算、儲存、通訊和依賴關係，對照硬體的容量、頻寬和算力做數量級估算。這類估算人容易出錯，AI 也一樣：只算權重讀取而忘了 KV 快取，按峰值算力推算速度而不查頻寬能否供給，把工作平分給多張卡卻遺漏卡間通訊，漏掉任何一項，結論都可能偏離幾倍甚至幾個數量級。估算還有另一層用意：讀博時導師張霖濤博士反覆叮囑，最佳化一定要做到物理所允許的極限。本書貫徹這一習慣，先按第一性原理算出硬體允許的上限，再看實測離上限還有多遠；差距不是模型漏了項，就是系統有可以去掉的開銷。從 FPGA 加速 Bing 搜尋排序、昇騰 AKG 運算元生成到 UB 萬卡互聯，我反覆遇到的是同一條線索： 資料搬移 。本書因此反覆追問五個問題： 搬什麼、搬多少、搬幾次、經過哪裡、誰必須等它。 更多寫作背景見 前言 。 目前書稿仍是初稿，正在持續修訂。 內容目錄 章 主題 主要問題 1 初識 AI Infra 一次生成需要多少視訊記憶體、計算和資料讀寫？ 2 模型架構 注意力、歷史狀態與專家結構如何改變系統需求？ 3 推理與訓練負載 任務階段、到達模式和狀態壽命如何影響資源需求？ 4 加速器架構 如何在計算、儲存、頻寬、功耗與成本之間取捨？ 5 運算元與執行時 融合、複用、併發和排程如何減少執行開銷？ 6 超節點 多裝置協作如何平衡容量、吞吐和同步代價？ 7 資料中心網路 網路頻寬、通訊方式和擁塞如何影響計算效率？ 8 推理最佳化 批處理、KV 管理、卸載與推測解碼何時有效？ 9 分散式推理 如何放置計算和狀態，並處理擴縮容與恢復？ 10 訓練系統 如何安排視訊記憶體、通訊和重算，讓訓練更高效？ 11 資源排程與執行環境 模型服務和工具環境如何共享資源，減少等待？ 12 端邊雲協同 任務放在本地、邊緣還是雲端，如何兼顧效果、延遲和成本？ 適合誰讀 如果你已經呼叫過模型 API，或在自己的機器上執行過模型，想進一步弄清模型為什麼慢、如何降低成本，這本書可以作為起點。從事系統、網路和晶片工作的工程師，以及相關方向的研究人員和學生，也能從書中看到各層設計與實際模型任務的聯絡。 閱讀時需要一些 Python、線性代數和計算機系統基礎，具體要求見 前言 。建議先讀第 1—3 章，瞭解模型與負載，再根據自己的興趣選擇重點： 做模型應用和推理服務，可以重點讀第 8、9 章，再看第 11、12 章的任務環境與部署；遇到容量、運算元或通訊問題時，回到第 4—7 章追蹤原因。 做系統或網路，可以重點讀第 5—7 章，再看第 9、10 章，檢查這些機制如何影響分散式推理與訓練。 做晶片與體系結構，可以重點讀第 4—7 章，並結合後續章節的任務算例，檢查硬體指標如何轉化為實際的服務能力。 希望系統學習，可以按目錄順序閱讀，配合計算工具和實驗，逐步核對自己的理解。 遇到書中的算例，不妨先自己估一下，再看推導和實驗結果。也可以換成你正在使用的模型和硬體，看看結論是否改變。 配套計算與實驗 配套計算工具 可以用來複算書中的數字，也可以換一組模型和輸入，估算資源需求。工具附有模型配置和 結果索引 ，靜態計算只需 Python 3.10+ 標準庫，無需 GPU 或模型權重。 git clone qwen3-8b --tokens 8192 --format md 倉庫使用 Git LFS 儲存論文和較大的輸入與測量記錄，合計約 20 GB。為避免克隆時全部下載， .lfsconfig 預設跳過所有 LFS 檔案，工作區中只留下指標；正文、配圖和靜態計算都不需要它們。復現某個實驗時，只下載對應目錄： git lfs install

title: HKUDS/AutoSwarm
abstract:
AutoSwarm: Unify All Your Agents. Break Context Barriers. 簡體中文 New: AutoSwarm Desktop Released — All Your Agents in One Private Workspace One window to coordinate agents, share context, review approvals, and track progress. Watch all your agents work together for you. What AutoSwarm does Why AutoSwarm? No single agent can do everything. You don’t need another agent—you need all your agents working as one. Different agents come with different: 🛠️ Capabilities — coding, research, browsing, office work, writing, computer use, and social networking; 🧠 Context and Memory — each agent maintains its own context, with little or no sharing across agents; ⚙️ Tools and Workflows — each agent follows its own interaction patterns and execution process; 🌐 Data and Application Ecosystems — agents are connected to different platforms, services, files, and data. Today, you are forced to switch interfaces, repeat information, coordinate subtasks, and manually combine results. AutoSwarm turns fragmented agents into one coordinated team. Give AutoSwarm a task once. It unifies all your agents into one coordinated team: Selects the right agents based on their capabilities; Shares context and memory across agents; Connects complementary tools and workflows; Bridges data and application ecosystems; Runs tasks in parallel for faster execution; Coordinates agent collaboration and keeps everyone aligned; Verifies and synthesizes results into one coherent answer. 🤖 Agents AutoSwarm Can Call Codex Claude Code OpenCode Cursor GitHub Copilot CLI Meta Muse Code CodeBuddy Hermes Nanobot DeepSeek Harness Grok Build Kimi Code AutoSwarm works across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Use AutoSwarm through: Desktop apps — AutoSwarm Desk for Windows and macOS (private assistant and live collaboration) Command-line interfaces (CLI) IDE extensions Skill-enabled agent environments The main host needs Skill support and local command execution. Collaborators need compatible local CLIs; your assistant can help connect missing ones. 🖥️ AutoSwarm Desk App 🚀 Easy to use One Lightweight Plug-in. Any Agent as Your Entry Point. All Your Agent at Work. How to Use AutoSwarm Give AutoSwarm to any agent you already use and ask: Install or update AutoSwarm for this agent. Reuse my existing configuration and verify which locally installed agents are available. Your assistant will report which collaborators are ready. To add another, tell it the agent's name; it will handle setup and verification. Then start any task with: Use AutoSwarm to read these 100 documents and summarize the key approaches and disagreements. AutoSwarm selects, connects, and coordinates the right agents for every task. 🤖 AutoSwarm in Action AutoSwarm.in.Action.mp4 📰 News AutoSwarm Desk for macOS is out : the same app on Apple silicon and Intel Macs, Python included. Apple silicon · Intel · Guide AutoSwarm Desk for Windows is out : a desktop app for AutoSwarm. Talk to a private assistant, start conversations with any of the twelve supported agents, follow how they share the work, and answer their approvals in one window. One installer, Python included, automatic updates. Download · Guide AutoSwarm is live! : Full technical details and multi-agent coordination algorithms are available in the archive . 🗺️ Roadmap -🔌 Expand Integrations — Support more agent products, models, tools, and native capabilities. -🤝 Improve Coordination — Strengthen context sharing, communication, task routing, and parallel execution. -🛡️ Enhance Reliability — Improve setup, monitoring, error recovery, verification, and overall user experience. 🌟 Citation If you find this work helpful to your research, please kindly consider citing our paper. @misc { li2026autoswarm , title = { AutoSwarm: Automating Agent Swarms } , author = { Zhonghang Li and Zongwei Li and Chao Huang } , year = { 2026 } , eprint = { 2610.33048 } } For agents: How to use AutoSwarm Installation and updates — instructions for the configuring agent (click to expand) Install Inspect the current host and existing Python 3.10+ / CLI installations. Reuse native models, credentials, proxy settings and project context. Ask before installing a missing provider CLI; configure only the agents needed. For a first installation, use git clone to obtain the official repository, then install the package and Skill for the current host . Reuse an existing checkout when available. Example for Codex: git clone https://github.com/HKUDS/AutoSwarm.git cd AutoSwarm
uv tool install --force . autoswarm setup --host codex Other host IDs: claude-code , opencode , cursor , copilot , muse , codebuddy , hermes , nanobot , dsh , grok , kimi . Without uv, use a dedicated Python 3.10+ environment and python -m pip install . ; keep its interpreter available. Do not reuse the archived v1 environment. Read the installed SKILL.md at the path returned by setup. It contains the launcher argv and usage instructions. Use that exact launcher when the App cannot find autoswarm . Run agents in the actual host environment; if needed, merge an existing CLI's absolute argv into providers.<provider>.command in the reported AutoSwarm home/config.json. Preserve unrelated settings. Verify requested providers in the actual project, replacing the example provider and directory as appropriate: autoswarm doctor --agent codex --probe --cwd /path/to/project Repeat --agent for several providers. This spends model calls to check a reply and native resume; verified: true confirms the probe. Version checks only establish executable discovery. An empty native authentication list does not prove that login is required. Handle pending native approvals/questions under the installed Skill's rules, then finish verification. Setup installs the Skill, its runtime and the host's integration. Follow the returned reload/trust instructions, then briefly name the verified collaborators and explain that the user can request others by name. If none are ready, propose connecting a suitable agent; obtain any missing installation authorization and handle configuration and verification. See configuration and recovery for native profiles, permissions and connection diagnostics. Update an existing installation Obtain the requested revision from the original source. For an existing Git checkout, preserve local edits, collect active delegated work, then run on the intended branch: git pull --ff-only
uv tool install --reinstall . autoswarm setup --host codex Use the actual host, existing AutoSwarm home and original installation destinations. Put --home <existing-home> before setup when needed; retain custom --skill-dir , --settings-file and --plugin-dir values. Refresh each host installation in use. For pip installations, use the existing dedicated interpreter to run python -m pip install --force-reinstall . , then python -m autoswarm setup --host codex with the same options. Run setup from the updated package : the installed Skill has its own runtime copy, so updating the checkout or package alone is insufficient. The old Skill launcher cannot fetch a new version. Keep configuration, records and native authentication, reload the host as required, read the refreshed Skill and verify the needed providers. Finish with the same brief collaborator summary as installation. There is no automatic updater. See upgrade details . Use and recover Follow the installed Skill to select agents, delegate ready work, collect results with wait --any , handle intermediate questions/approvals and verify deliverables before answering. Ordinary tasks use the current conversation; native wake-up is optional and needs a supported host binding. Read only the relevant references: capabilities and data scope , communication , native interactions , model selection . Diagnose retained calls and logs before retrying uncertain operations. title: PrefectHQ/fastmcp
abstract: FastMCP 🚀 Move fast and make things. Made with 💙 by Prefect The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects LLMs to tools and data. FastMCP is a full MCP application framework for servers, clients, and interactive apps. A server starts with ordinary Python: from fastmcp import FastMCP mcp = FastMCP ( "Demo 🚀" ) @ mcp . tool def add ( a : int , b : int ) -> int : """Add two numbers""" return a + b if __name__ == "__main__" : mcp . run () Why FastMCP Building an effective MCP application is harder than it looks. FastMCP handles all of it. Declare a tool with a Python function, and the schema, validation, and documentation are generated automatically. Connect to a server with a URL, and transport negotiation, authentication, and protocol lifecycle are managed for you. You focus on your logic, and the MCP part just works: with FastMCP, best practices are built in. That's why FastMCP is the standard framework for working with MCP. FastMCP 1.0 was incorporated into the official MCP Python SDK in 2024. Today, the actively maintained standalone project is downloaded a million times a day, and some version of FastMCP powers 70% of MCP servers across all languages. FastMCP has three pillars: Servers Expose tools, resources, and prompts to LLMs. Apps Give your tools interactive UIs rendered directly in the conversation. Clients Connect to any MCP server — local or remote, programmatic or CLI. Servers wrap your Python functions into MCP-compliant tools, resources, and prompts. Clients connect to any server with full protocol support. And Apps give your tools interactive UIs rendered directly in the conversation. Building in TypeScript? FastMCP for TypeScript is the official counterpart, built and maintained by the same team. Same pillars, same ideas, npm install @prefecthq/fastmcp-ts . Ready to build? Start with the installation guide or jump straight to the quickstart . Scale MCP with FastMCP Gateway FastMCP handles the MCP application layer. FastMCP Gateway is the enterprise MCP gateway for scaling servers and tools across teams, with centralized governance over how they are deployed, discovered, secured, and used. FastMCP and FastMCP Gateway are built by the same team at Prefect . Deploy FastMCP servers from GitHub with branch previews and instant rollback. Create a private registry of every MCP your company uses. Secure access with SSO and tool-level RBAC. Get audit logs, observability, and governance across your MCP stack. Remix approved tools into purpose-built endpoints for teams and agents. Start with FastMCP. Scale with FastMCP Gateway → Installation We recommend adding FastMCP to your project with uv : uv add fastmcp For full installation instructions, including verification and upgrading, see the Installation Guide . Upgrading? We have guides for: Upgrading from FastMCP 3 Upgrading from FastMCP 2 Upgrading from MCP SDK v1 or v2 Upgrading from the low-level SDK v1 or v2 📚 Documentation FastMCP's complete documentation is available at gofastmcp.com , including detailed guides, API references, and advanced patterns. Documentation is also available in llms.txt format , which is a simple markdown standard that LLMs can consume easily: llms.txt is essentially a sitemap, listing all the pages in the documentation. llms-full.txt contains the entire documentation. Note this may exceed the context window of your LLM. Give your coding agent llms.txt as its starting point. See Coding Agents for version-matched documentation and the optional server authoring skill. Community: Join our Discord server to connect with other FastMCP developers and share what you're building. Contributing Start with CONTRIBUTING.md for accepted contributions and the issue-assignment workflow, then follow the Contributing Guide for setup and validation. Agents should read AGENTS.md .

title: ManimCommunity/manim
abstract:
An animation engine for explanatory math videos Manim is an animation engine for explanatory math videos. It's used to create precise animations programmatically, as demonstrated in the videos of 3Blue1Brown . Note The community edition of Manim (ManimCE) is a version maintained and developed by the community. It was forked from 3b1b/manim, a tool originally created and open-sourced by Grant Sanderson, also creator of the 3Blue1Brown educational math videos. While Grant Sanderson continues to maintain his own repository, we recommend this version for its continued development, improved features, enhanced documentation, and more active community-driven maintenance. If you would like to study how Grant makes his videos, head over to his repository ( 3b1b/manim ). Table of Contents: Installation Usage Documentation Docker Help with Manim Contributing License Installation Caution These instructions are for the community version only . Trying to use these instructions to install 3b1b/manim or instructions there to install this version will cause problems. Read this and decide which version you wish to install, then only follow the instructions for your desired version. Manim requires a few dependencies that must be installed prior to using it. If you
want to try it out first before installing it locally, you can do so in our online Jupyter environment . For local installation, please visit the Documentation and follow the appropriate instructions for your operating system. Usage Manim is an extremely versatile package. The following is an example Scene you can construct: from manim import * class SquareToCircle ( Scene ): def construct ( self ): circle = Circle () square = Square () square . flip ( RIGHT ) square . rotate ( - 3 * TAU / 8 ) circle . set_fill ( PINK , opacity = 0.5 ) self . play ( Create ( square )) self . play ( Transform ( square , circle )) self . play ( FadeOut ( square )) In order to view the output of this scene, save the code in a file called example.py . Then, run the following in a terminal window: manim -p -ql example.py SquareToCircle You should see your native video player program pop up and play a simple scene in which a square is transformed into a circle. You may find some more simple examples within this GitHub repository . You can also visit the official gallery for more advanced examples. Manim also ships with a %%manim IPython magic which allows to use it conveniently in JupyterLab (as well as classic Jupyter) notebooks. See the corresponding documentation for some guidance and try it out online . Command line arguments The general usage of Manim is as follows: The -p flag in the command above is for previewing, meaning the video file will automatically open when it is done rendering. The -ql flag is for a faster rendering at a lower quality. Some other useful flags include: -s to skip to the end and just show the final frame. -n <number> to skip ahead to the n 'th animation of a scene. -f show the file in the file browser. For a thorough list of command line arguments, visit the documentation . Documentation Documentation is in progress at ReadTheDocs . Docker The community also maintains a docker image ( manimcommunity/manim ), which can be found on DockerHub .
Instructions on how to install and use it can be found in our documentation . Help with Manim If you need help installing or using Manim, feel free to reach out to our Discord
Server or Reddit Community . If you would like to submit a bug report or feature request, please open an issue. Contributing Contributions to Manim are always welcome. In particular, there is a dire need for tests and documentation. For contribution guidelines, please see the documentation . However, please note that Manim is currently undergoing a major refactor. In general,
contributions implementing new features will not be accepted in this period.
The contribution guide may become outdated quickly; we highly recommend joining our Discord server to discuss any potential
contributions and keep up to date with the latest developments. Most developers on the project use uv for management. You'll want to have uv installed and available in your environment.
Learn more about uv at its documentation and find out how to install manim with uv at the manim dev-installation guide in the manim documentation. How to Cite Manim We acknowledge the importance of good software to support research, and we note
that research becomes more valuable when it is communicated effectively. To
demonstrate the value of Manim, we ask that you cite Manim in your work.
Currently, the best way to cite Manim is to go to our repository page (if you aren't already) and
click the "cite this repository" button on the right sidebar. This will generate
a citation in your preferred format, and will also integrate well with citation managers. Code of Conduct Our full code of conduct, and how we enforce it, can be read on our website . title: Canner/WrenAI
abstract:
Open-source GenBI for AI agents Your agents generate governed SQL, deploy dashboards, and keep business definitions in Git, across 22+ data sources. Get started in 3 commands ↓ · Read the docs → · Join Discord → What WrenAI is WrenAI is the open-source generative BI (GenBI) engine . It gives the AI agents you already use (Claude Code, Cursor, MCP clients, LangChain) a governed semantic layer and an AI context layer , so they turn business questions into correct SQL, ship the answer as a shareable dashboard, and stay inside your guardrails. Schemas tell an agent where data lives. Wren tells it what the data means : approved metric definitions, enums, units, joins, worked examples, and the tribal knowledge buried in docs and chat threads. All of it lives as reviewable YAML and Markdown in a repo you own. Quickstart Three commands, then your agent does the rest. Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Codex, and 50+ other agents . 1. Install the CLI pip install wrenai Add connector extras as you need them, for example pip install "wrenai[postgres,memory]" . 2. Teach your agent about Wren npx skills add Canner/WrenAI This installs a ~50-line discovery stub. Your agent fetches full workflow guides from the CLI on demand, so instructions always match the installed version. 3. Open your agent in a project folder and ask "Use Wren to set up my Postgres database." The agent checks your environment, creates a connection profile, scaffolds the project, and runs a first query. No database handy? Say "Use Wren with the bundled jaffle_shop sample" and run the same flow against a real sample warehouse. Slow pip install from mainland China? pip install wrenai -i https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple If HuggingFace model downloads time out, run export HF_ENDPOINT=https://hf-mirror.com before using the CLI. Then keep going Once you're connected, these three prompts cover the whole GenBI loop: Beat Ask your agent What happens Know "Enrich my Wren project with the business context in raw/ ." Runs wren skills get enrich-context . Writes definitions, examples, and memory as reviewable files. Generate "Who are our top 10 customers by sales this quarter?" Recalls MDL context and past queries, writes governed SQL, executes via wren query . Deploy "Turn that into a dashboard I can filter and share, deployed to Vercel." Runs wren skills get genbi . Builds a browser-side app and returns a live URL on your Vercel or Cloudflare Pages account. Follow the full quickstart → · Build & deploy a GenBI app → Why agent builders pick WrenAI Answers and dashboards, not just SQL. Generate a governed answer, deploy it as a dashboard, share the URL. One agent-driven loop, end to end. Correct instead of confidently wrong. Schema-aware retrieval, MDL planning, dry-plan validation, row limits, value profiling, and structured errors with hints keep agent SQL inside guardrails. Business meaning lives in Git. Metric definitions, enums, approved joins, and proven examples are versioned files. Review them in a pull request. Diff them. Take them with you. Works through the agents you already run. Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Codex, MCP clients, LangChain. Wren is a layer, not another chat UI to adopt. Sits on your existing stack. Warehouse, transformation pipelines, existing semantic models. 22+ sources on one Apache DataFusion engine. Open by default. Core engine, SDK, and skills under Apache-2.0. It runs without us. How Wren compares A raw LLM agent A traditional BI tool A bare semantic layer WrenAI Writes SQL for you ✅ (often wrong) ❌ ❌ ✅ governed Knows your business definitions ❌ partial, in-tool ✅ (schema only) ✅ + non-schema knowledge Generates & deploys dashboards ❌ ✅ (manual, in-tool) ❌ ✅ agent-driven Works through your agents (Claude Code, Cursor, MCP…) ✅ ❌ ❌ ✅ Open, reviewable, Git-friendly context ❌ ❌ partial ✅ Governed execution across 22+ sources ❌ per-connector ✅ (definitions only) ✅ Wren is for you if… You want AI agents to produce trustworthy BI , answers and dashboards, not just plausible SQL. Your business logic (definitions, enums, units, approved joins) lives outside the database and your agents keep getting it wrong. You want a context layer that is open, reviewable, and version-controlled , usable by every agent and every person, not gated behind one vendor's UI. Skip Wren if you only need a one-off chart from a single CSV, or you're happy letting an agent guess at SQL with no governance. Take it to your team with git push Everything Wren writes on your laptop is plain YAML and Markdown in a repo you own. Git Sync turns that same repo into a governed, team-wide GenBI deployment in Wren Cloud or a self-hosted installation, including air-gapped. Nothing to export, nothing to re-model. abstract: FreeLLMAPI 10.1 billion tokens per month.  87 free LLM providers. 1,313 free model endpoints. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Aggregate free tiers from dozens of providers, plus custom OpenAI-compatible chat, embedding, image, and audio endpoints, behind a single /v1 API. Keys are stored encrypted. Free installs get the monthly snapshot, so a model reaches them 30 days after it joins the live feed; premium routers get it the same day. Go live at freellmapi.co ($19/yr, cancel anytime). Contents Why this exists Supported providers Compatible CLIs & coding agents How it compares Features Quick start Desktop app Works with OpenAI-compatible clients Languages Premium (live catalog) Using the API Screenshots How it works FAQ Limitations Contributing Disclaimer Guides: Install & deploy · API reference · Clients & coding agents · Prompt compression · Architecture & internals · Documentation index · Contributor guide Why this exists Every serious AI lab now offers a free tier, a few million tokens a month, a few thousand requests a day. On its own each tier is a toy. Stacked together, they add up to roughly 10.1 billion tokens per month of working inference capacity, across 736 model families / 1,313 provider endpoints from small-and-fast to reasonably capable. The problem is that stacking them by hand is painful: eighty-seven different SDKs, eighty-seven different rate limits, eighty-seven places a request can fail. FreeLLMAPI collapses that into one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Point any OpenAI client library at your local server, and it routes transparently across whichever providers you've added keys for. And the free-tier landscape shifts weekly: providers launch models, retire them, and change quotas without notice. FreeLLMAPI tracks all of that for you. The router pulls a signed model catalog from freellmapi.co on its own, so your install keeps up without a git pull . See Premium (live catalog) for how fast it keeps up. The full, always-current list lives at freellmapi.co/models with per-model rate limits, context windows, and free-token budgets. Compatible CLIs & coding agents Claude Code Codex CLI Gemini CLI Cursor Cline Roo Code OpenCode Aider … plus Continue, Goose, Qwen Code, Kilo Code, Crush, Zed, JetBrains AI, DeepSeek Harness, MiMo Code, AtomCode, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, Reasonix, ZCode and any OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Gemini or Ollama client Most agents configure themselves with one command that reads your live catalog, backs up the existing config and merges into it: npx freellmapi setup-claude --url http://localhost:3001 --api-key < unified-key > All supported agents and their setup commands → · Per-tool recipes, MCP server and URL tokens → How it compares Based on public documentation, July 2026 — corrections welcome. Features Every OpenAI-style surface — /v1/chat/completions , /v1/responses (what Codex CLI needs), /v1/completions (editor ghost-text autocomplete), /v1/images/generations , /v1/videos/generations , /v1/audio/speech , /v1/audio/transcriptions , /v1/embeddings , and /v1/models — streaming and non-streaming, from the official SDKs or any OpenAI-compatible client. Details → Native Gemini + Ollama surfaces — Gemini CLI can use /v1beta ( generateContent , streaming, token counting, models), while opt-in Ollama emulation serves NDJSON chat/generate, tags, metadata, and embeddings for Zed, JetBrains, and other local-model clients. Fusion (multi-model synthesis) — request the virtual fusion model and the router fans your prompt out to a panel of diverse free models in parallel, then a judge model synthesizes one answer from the drafts. Details → Image, video & speech generation — /v1/images/generations , /v1/videos/generations , and /v1/audio/speech route across the providers that serve media models; images and speech also accept custom OpenAI-compatible media endpoints. Video jobs are normalized across synchronous and queued providers and return a completed MP4. Tool calling & structured outputs — OpenAI-style tools round-trip across providers (plain-text tool calls are rescued into real tool_calls ), plus response_format , seed , logprobs , penalties, and the rest of the sampling params passed through per provider. Smart routing, six strategies — live per-model speed/capability/reliability scores rank your chain; automatic fallover retries the next model on 429/5xx with cooldowns and key rotation. Routing in detail → Unified models & profiles — the same model on several providers collapses into one entry with strict in-group failover; named fallback-chain profiles (a coding chain, a vision chain) switch from the dashboard or per request via auto:<profile> , and custom chains can be renamed in place from the chain manager. Per-key rate tracking — RPM/RPD/TPM/TPD counters per (platform, model, key) that learn providers' reported ceilings, so routing always stays under every cap. Self-updating model catalog — the router syncs a signed catalog from freellmapi.co twice a day: new models, quota changes, and provider quirk fixes land automatically. Free installs track the monthly snapshot, which each model joins 30 days after it lands in the live feed; premium routers get it same-day. Details → Prompt compression (opt-in) — a shared, fail-open request pipeline can deduplicate prompts, filter tool output, compact repeated JSON, and trim stale context before cache lookup and routing. Details → Encrypted keys, one token out — provider keys are AES-256-GCM encrypted in SQLite and decrypted in-memory per request; your apps only ever see a single unified freellmapi-… bearer token. Admin dashboard & analytics — React UI to manage keys, reorder the chain, run a playground, and read p50/p95/TTFT analytics over 24h–90d windows; login-gated, dark/light themes, 60 languages . ChatGPT-ready MCP server & interactive docs — ChatGPT and other MCP clients can call FreeLLMAPI inference, list usable models, inspect provider health/usage/cache/routing metadata, and manage the routing strategy over /mcp ; a dependency-free OpenAPI viewer lives at /v1/docs . Install & deploy → Runs anywhere Node 20+ runs — Windows, macOS, Linux servers, or a small ARM SBC (Raspberry Pi included). ~40 MB RSS at idle behind PM2 / systemd / whatever supervisor you prefer. title: harry0703/MangoDisk
abstract: MangoDisk Disk cleanup, storage analysis, and privacy protection for macOS , Windows , and Linux English · 簡體中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Русский What MangoDisk Can Do Storage 1. Deep Cleanup Recover storage used by everyday apps, development work, and AI tools. Find caches, build artifacts, and local models in one place, without hunting through hidden folders: System and user caches : Reclaim space taken up over time by system temporary files, diagnostic data, and rebuildable caches. Application caches : Keep application caches, logs, update packages, and temporary content from quietly consuming more and more storage. Browser data : Reclaim space used by cached and temporary web data from Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, Arc, Opera, and other browsers. Developer tools and Xcode : Quickly recover substantial storage used by package managers, IDEs, compiler caches, and Xcode development data. Container caches : Free up space used by inactive build caches and rebuildable data from Docker and other container tools. Project build artifacts : Recover space used by rebuildable dependencies, caches, and build directories across Node.js, Rust, Gradle, Swift, Python, .NET, Godot, CMake, and other projects. AI tools : Reclaim space taken up by caches, old logs, and temporary downloads from tools such as ChatGPT, Codex, and Claude, without tracking down each tool's data folders. AI models : See how much space local models from Ollama, LM Studio, Hugging Face, and ComfyUI use, and remove those you no longer need to make room for new models and everyday files. Models are selected manually and must be downloaded again if needed later. Application optimization : Shrink supported applications without affecting normal use, leaving more room on your disk. Smart recommendations help you make safe choices quickly. You can also review items individually and see the estimated reclaimable space upfront, keeping every cleanup predictable and under your control. 2. Large File Cleanup Quickly find the largest files and reclaim space used by old installers, videos, archives, and other bulky content without digging through folders one by one. 3. Duplicate File Cleanup Reclaim space taken up by duplicate copies without treating files as duplicates just because they share a name. Smart selection keeps at least one file in every group, so cleanup stays effortless and safe. 4. Disk Space Analysis See where your disk space is going at a glance. Switch between a treemap and a sunburst chart , and choose how many levels to display to explore space usage and folder structure. Browse folders alongside the file list to quickly find the largest folders and files and decide what to clean up. Privacy & Security 5. Privacy Cleanup Keep browsing history, searches, cookies, recent items, and clipboard data from lingering on your computer. Clear traces left by browsers, applications, and the system to reduce exposure of your activity and make everyday privacy easier to manage. System Tools 6. Application Uninstall and Cleanup Uninstall applications and clear related caches, settings, and leftovers so removing an application actually gives you the space back. Potential personal files are handled cautiously to reduce the risk of accidental deletion. 7. Startup Item Management Reduce unnecessary startup delays and background resource use, so your computer starts faster and feels lighter. Turn items back on at any time when you need them again. 8. System Optimization Reduce unnecessary settings that slow down your system or get in the way. Balance performance, privacy, and personal preferences so your computer feels faster and easier to use. 9. System Maintenance Fix common problems like missing search results, incorrect icons, no sound, or network connection failures—without hunting down fixes or typing complex commands. Get your computer back to normal sooner. 10. Context Menus (Windows) Available since version 1.2.3 Keep right-click menus tidy and easy to use. Browse entries by menu location or app, disable, restore or remove supported items, and adjust menus for individual file types. Add everyday actions such as copying paths and opening a terminal, along with shortcuts to system tools. Activity 11. Operation History Keep a clear record of every cleanup and system change. See how much space you recovered, what completed successfully, and whether anything still needs your attention. Resource Usage and Memory Management Available since version 1.1.1 Track CPU, GPU, memory, network speeds and disk activity in real time, with trends to help you understand resource use. On supported devices, you can also check temperatures, power usage, battery status and disk health. Quickly find resource-heavy apps, quit those you no longer need, and free memory manually or automatically. Display metrics in the menu bar, taskbar, system tray or a floating desktop window. Customize the content and appearance to keep an eye on your computer without opening the main window. AI Explanations Available since version 1.1.0 Unsure what an item does or what might happen if you change it? AI explanations use the item's description and current scan results to explain its purpose and what to consider before taking action. Spend less time looking things up and make more informed choices. Get explanations directly from items in Deep Cleanup (built-in rules), Privacy Cleanup, Startup Item Management, System Optimization, and System Maintenance. Official releases include free explanations each day, with the option to connect your own AI service. AI offers guidance; you decide which actions to take. Safety and Rules Important MangoDisk puts data safety ahead of reclaiming more space. Cleanup rules and system optimizations only ship after their safety boundaries are clearly defined and they pass validation on real systems. MangoDisk scans in read-only mode by default. Before cleanup, deletion, uninstall, or system setting changes begin, you can review and confirm exactly what will happen. Results are saved to Operation History. System Optimization only uses built-in, validated settings. It never accepts arbitrary registry paths, terminal commands, or scripts. MangoDisk reads each setting again after changing it and calls out high-impact items and changes that require administrator access or a restart. MangoDisk maintains its own cleanup rules. All AI-generated code should be Open Source
abstract:
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why. First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering. The second reason is legal: purely AI -generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute , which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI . Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI -generated images to be tagged as Public Domain . However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI -generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license. Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source. According to the latest findings, it appears that we were led to believe that there was an organic supply shortage, but in reality, we learn that Jensen was actually leveraging NVIDIA’s own balance sheet to finance AI startups and datacenter buildouts so they could absorb the company’s over-ordered semiconductor shipments from TSMC. NVIDIA faced an “avalanche” of excess TSMC silicon and memory, and the only way to curb the oversupply was to fund AI startups The fresh revelations stem from a tense August 2026 confrontation between Huang and NVIDIA’s longtime Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, now the interim CEO. Seeing as how the former head honcho was escalating the GPU maker’s financial exposure, Kress pushed to rein in the company’s “circular financing” commitments to smaller cloud providers and major AI firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic, according to The Wall Street Journal. Initial discussions had floated underwriting roughly 8 gigawatts of OpenAI compute valued at up to $250 billion, and Kress successfully scaled NVIDIA’s signed guarantee cap down to roughly 4.25 gigawatts, or up to $125 billion. As a result, Jensen reportedly belittled Kress for questioning the deals, referring to her as “a deer in the headlights.” To justify NVIDIA's need to financially underwrite OpenAI and smaller cloud operators to keep them purchasing its GPUs, Huang privately admitted that major cloud giants were pivoting away from NVIDIA in favor of in-house custom chips. With hyperscalers actively reducing their reliance on “off-the-shelf parts,” Huang acknowledged that the massive volume of prepaid TSMC wafers and memory NVIDIA had committed to buying was “coming at him like an avalanche.” By funding datacenter expansion for AI startups, NVIDIA effectively created artificial demand to clear out its own surplus silicon instead of letting the supply flood the market and force GPU prices down. Those internal pressures align with earlier assessments from industry analyst Ed Zitron, who estimated that at least $200 billion worth of NVIDIA AI GPUs are sitting idle in warehouses after being purchased by cloud giants that lacked either the electrical grid capacity or immediate end-user demand to power them on. Amazon faced a similar dilemma . Knowing that the imminent avalanche would be upon NVIDIA sooner rather than later, the company reportedly contacted TSMC to wind down its upcoming chip orders. For PC builders and hardware enthusiasts who have endured years of steep GPU and RAM pricing under the impression of severe component scarcity, the disclosures shatter the shortage narrative and expose the aggressive financial maneuvering used to keep hardware prices elevated. While Jensen can’t be faulted for making these moves because he was keeping the best interests of the company in mind, it’s a stab in the back for gamers and hardware owners who are unable to locate any mouth-watering deals for GPUs or memory because of the perceived shortage.
