title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why'd it get the midterms so wrong?
abstract:
The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment. What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else. In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die. Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand. There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats. In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.” “Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida , they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones. Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next. Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

title: US IRS free online tax filing open source repo (2025)
abstract:
Direct File Direct File is a service from the United States Government that provides taxpayers the option to electronically file their federal tax return for free, directly with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Direct File is an interview-based service that is intended to work as well on a mobile phone as it does on a laptop, tablet, or desktop computer. It is available in English and Spanish and is designed to be accessible to taxpayers who have a variety of attitudes, aptitudes, abilities, and access needs. Direct File interprets the United States' Internal Revenue Code (26 USC) as plain language questions, the answers to which should be known to taxpayers without need of external instructions or publications. Taxpayers' answers are then translated into standard tax forms and transmitted to the IRS's Modernized e-File (MeF) API, which is available for authorized public use. These questions and logic, developed in close collaboration with the IRS Office of Chief Counsel , as well as the associated test cases and scenarios, may be useful for others working on products that need to accurately interpret United States tax law as of Tax Year 2024. Direct File also incorporates the Fact Graph, a declarative, XML-based knowledge graph data structure that is designed to reason about incomplete information, such as a partially completed tax return. The Fact Graph is written in the Scala programming language; it runs on the JVM on the backend and is transpiled via Scala.js to run on the client as well. Direct File's Fact Graph is not domain-specific, and it may be useful to revenue agencies and as a reference for business rules engine implementations. Although Direct File only files federal tax returns, United States taxpayers also have state and local filing obligations. Direct File facilitates the completion of these obligations by enabling taxpayers to optionally import their federal return data into a third-party tool that can file state and/or local taxes, without needing to reenter information. This transaction is enabled via a State API, which transfers both standard MeF XML as well as an enriched JSON format that includes additional data elements that were identified as being useful to state revenue agencies to streamline the state tax experience. Direct File was developed by an in-house team of technologists at the IRS. The blended, cross-agency team included support from USDS and GSA , as well as vendor teams TrussWorks , Coforma , and ATI . For a more details on the program and its history see https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p5969.pdf and https://www.irs.gov/filing/irs-direct-file-for-free This repository has been archived and is no longer maintained. The code is provided for historical reference and may contain unpatched or unknown vulnerabilities. It should not be used in production systems. Where do I start? title: TRANSLATING POWER: AI, MEDIATION AND THE IMAGINARY OF MANIPULATION IN ACADEMIC CONTEXTS
abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence in academic writing and translation is changing not only the speed of textual production but also the ways in which linguistic authority is constructed and perceived. In multilingual academic contexts, AI systems translate, reformulate, and refine texts according to dominant conventions of academic English. Such assistance may widen access to international communication, yet its fluency can also make the interpretative choices embedded in the resulting text less visible. This article examines AI-mediated Romanian-English academic translation as a site where linguistic assistance, symbolic power, and the imaginary of manipulation intersect. The study approaches translation as mediation rather than neutral transfer. It asks how AI may reshape lexical authority, epistemic stance, and stylistic identity, how these changes influence the perceived legitimacy of academic discourse, and when unobtrusive mediation may acquire a potentially manipulative effect. The theoretical discussion connects translation studies with scholarship on symbolic power, academic stance, and sociotechnical imaginaries. Methodologically, the article adopts a conceptual qualitative approach supported by three illustrative Romanian-English micro-analyses. These examples are not treated as a representative corpus and do not support statistical generalisation. Instead, they reveal how apparently minor lexical, epistemic, and stylistic reformulations can influence authority, certainty, and authorial visibility. The article argues that manipulation should not be equated automatically with factual distortion or deliberate ideological intent. It may also arise through naturalisation, when a fluent and plausible formulation is accepted as transparent or inevitable. The article concludes that responsible AI-assisted academic translation requires comparison with the source, attention to shifts in certainty, agency and rhetorical positioning, and clear human responsibility for the final text. For translators, writers and educators, critical AI literacy entails treating generated language as a proposal to be evaluated rather than as an impersonal solution.

title: VLM-DC: Vision--Language Model for Automotive Data Collection
abstract: The development of advanced driver-assistance systems (ADASs) and autonomous driving technologies depends on high-quality, representative driving data. Traditional collection methods either demand extensive manual filtering or rely on rigid thresholds that miss critical edge cases. To overcome these limitations and meet diverse operational and system requirements, this work introduces a two-module, vision–language model (VLM)-based framework for intelligent and targeted data collection. The first module employs a cloud–edge multiagent architecture, where a cloud-based large language model (LLM) coordinates sensor selection and an edge-deployed VLM evaluates scene relevance. This approach achieves 91.35% overall precision, reduces storage by 28.30%, and shows promising performance on geographically distinct out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. The second module implements a distributed VLM architecture with knowledge distillation (KD), deploying a lightweight vision encoder on vehicles and a language decoder in the cloud. A selective token transfer mechanism reduces model size by 71% and bandwidth use by 50% while maintaining 91.86% overall accuracy. Both modules outperform larger baselines while remaining computationally and communication efficient. Overall, this framework shifts automotive data collection from exhaustive recording to selective capture of valuable driving moments, accelerating ADAS development and validation.

title: A new hash function based on irreversible finite automata
abstract: A mathematical hash function maps inputs of arbitrary length to unique outputs (digests) of a fixed length. It is highly useful and used in almost all information security applications; it can also serve as index data in hash tables, detect duplicate data for fingerprinting or uniquely identifying files, and serve as well for checksums to identify data corruption. In this work, a novel 256-bit cryptographic hash function based on the irreversible Mealy finite automata model (IFA) is introduced. In this architecture, the irreversible transition matrix of the Mealy automaton (IFA) is constructed using a non-injective state-transition mechanism to introduce local irreversibility and ambiguous backward reconstruction. The automaton output table is precomputed using a Chebyshev-based nonlinear generator to improve output randomness and nonlinear complexity. For further diffusion, confusion, collision resistance, and one-wayness improvements, we integrate the irreversible automaton within a sponge-based construction with a 512-bit internal state (256-bit rate + 256-bit capacity), yielding a designed collision resistance of bits and preimage resistance of under the sponge capacity bound. Evaluation against SHA-256 shows an avalanche mean of 50.02% (σ = 3.14%), all 13 NIST SP 800-22 statistical tests passed, and zero collisions among 50,000 tests. Throughput is about 13 MB/s versus 183 MB/s for SHA-256, reflecting the sequential dependency of the Mealy transformation.

title: Cybercrime law and digital forensics: adapting legal frameworks for future technologies
abstract: Linked authenticity, integrity, reliability, attribution, jurisdiction, and privacy challenges are created by digital evidence from cloud platforms, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs), biometrics, drones, blockchain, and virtual environments. This review synthesizes scholarly and authoritative sources on cybercrime law, digital forensics, and emerging technologies through a structured narrative review. The review reveals a technical–legal divide: it emphasizes investigative efficiency, while acquisition, hashing, metadata, chain of custody, tool validation, and automated-analysis reliability require clarification for evidentiary scrutiny. Technology, evidence source, forensic challenge, legal risk, admissibility requirement, and governance response are linked through the Technology–Forensic–Legal Admissibility (TFLA) Framework. Primary artifacts are distinguished from analytical outputs; technical weaknesses are translated into legal consequences and safeguards. Standards and evidentiary rules are complemented; TFLA is conceptual, not empirically validated. Technology-neutral, technically informed, rights-compliant governance is supported through transparent documentation, corroboration, human oversight, and institutional competence. Digital-forensic system design is linked to trustworthy technology governance.

title: An Occlusion-Aware Decision-Making Framework With Cooperative Active Perception for Connected Automated Vehicles in Unsignalized Intersections
abstract: Occlusions at unsignalized intersections can hide safety-critical traffic participants and force autonomous vehicles (AVs) into overly conservative or unsafe decisions. Although cooperative perception among connected automated vehicles (CAVs) can partially alleviate this issue, its effectiveness remains limited because CAVs typically conduct passive sensing, which often leaves many risky occluded areas unresolved. This article proposes an occlusion-aware decision-making framework for CAVs considering cooperative active perception (CAP). It first conducts occlusion modeling using a directed-graph road representation and phantom vehicle model, which identifies risky occluded areas through conflict-point reasoning, spatiotemporal reachability analysis, and passive cooperative perception among CAVs. Remaining unobservable risky occlusions trigger active perception requests to nearby CAVs. Assisted CAVs then employ a finite-state-machine policy to select safe viewpoint-enhancing maneuvers based on surrounding traffic, occlusion type, and request urgency. In addition, the ego CAV plans conservatively using worst case reachable sets for phantom occluded vehicles before the remaining risky occluded areas are revealed, and upon receiving occlusion information, switches to selecting a safe speed range that enables efficient traversal. Simulation results and real-time co-simulation on dSPACE, a commercial high-fidelity vehicle-system validation platform, demonstrate that the proposed strategy can potentially improve computational efficiency and provide safe and efficient driving in unsignalized intersections.

title: GA-LLMSS: Text-Spatio–Temporal Graph-Guided and Cross-Modal Alignment-Enhanced Large Language Model Empowered Soft Sensor
abstract: Data-driven soft sensing has gained widespread application in modern industrial processes for real-time, low-cost estimation of key quality variables, but existing models are generally constrained by single-modal numerical inputs and limited representational generalization. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in time-series tasks due to their sequence-pattern generalization, textual reasoning, and cross-modal knowledge transfer abilities, yet their application in soft sensing remains limited. To bridge this gap, this article proposes a text-spatio–temporal graph-guided and cross-modal alignment-enhanced LLM-empowered two-stage soft sensor (GA-LLMSS). Specifically, a scale-adaptive spatio–temporal graph encoder (SASTGE) is developed, which reconstructs raw multivariate time series into dynamic spatio–temporal interaction graphs (STIGs) according to the nonstationary characteristics, injecting structured prior logic to compensate for LLMs’ inherent deficiency in intervariable spatial perception. Building on this, a prompt-enhanced graph construction (PEGC) module enriches input semantics by crafting industrial prior knowledge prompts (IPKPs) with higher-order statistics, while an anchor token then serves as a cross-modal hub to establish logic-guided edges between prompts and graph nodes that explicitly guide LLMs in capturing cross-modal logical relationships and maintaining semantic coherence. To bridge textual and time-series modalities, an improved representation learning, dropout autoregressive alignment stage (DAAS), is proposed to enforce learning of deep spatio–temporal couplings from incomplete observations. Finally, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts the model to real-world industrial scenarios: air preheaters (APs) and gas turbines (GTs). Experiments show that GA-LLMSS achieves advanced accuracy, superior few-shot representation generalization, and ablation studies validate the independent contributions of each key module.

title: Brain Cognition-Inspired Adaptable LLM Agents for Continuous Knowledge Reuse Across Tasks in IoT
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are promising in Internet of Things (IoT) applications. However, existing agent systems suffer from an ephemeral limitation: agents are instantiated for individual tasks and terminated upon completion, losing valuable execution experiences across different tasks where past knowledge reuse is impossible. Inspired by dual-process theory in cognitive science, we propose a brain cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse across heterogeneous task streams, termed the cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse (CIA-CKR). The CIA-CKR framework separates fast (reactive execution) from slow (deliberative planning) cognition phases by maintaining a persistent knowledge base throughout the operational lifetime of agents. Two synergistic mechanisms are designed that mirror bidirectional knowledge flow in human cognition: a personalized agent generation mechanism that retrieves task-relevant knowledge and configures context-specific agent capabilities through top-down adaptation, and a knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts experiential insights from execution traces through bottom-up feedback. Extensive experiments on HomeBench (smart home control) and OmniEAR (embodied multiagent collaboration) datasets demonstrate that CIA-CKR consistently outperforms both vanilla LLMs and recent memory-augmented methods, achieving 10.82% and 4.23% average accuracy improvements on HomeBench and OmniEAR, respectively, over the best baselines.
